title: Multi-Cycle Datapath and Control
subtitle: One step per clock cycle, shared hardware, and a state machine in charge.

objectives: Explain why the single-cycle processor is not ideal
Describe the five steps of the multi-cycle processor and what each does

steps.question: In Class 10 every instruction, even a simple add, waited for the slowest one. Could each instruction use only the time it needs?
clues: Split every instruction into **short steps**, one per clock cycle.
Let steps **share** one memory and one ALU.
A **state machine** decides which step comes next.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: Three problems with single-cycle

items: **The clock is set by the slowest instruction** (lw), so every instruction pays for it
**Hardware is duplicated**: two memories, a main ALU and two extra adders, each used once per cycle
**No flexibility**: a long operation such as multiply would stretch the clock for everybody

steps.why: Single-cycle is simple, but it wastes both time and hardware.
steps.real: Early simple processors used designs like this; faster ones changed the structure rather than only the speed.

explainAgain.beginner: A school bus that waits for the slowest student at every stop, even when most are ready.

steps.title: The multi-cycle idea

nodes.label: Fetch
nodes.note: Memory is read; PC + 4 is computed.

nodes.label: Decode
nodes.note: Register file read; control sees the opcode.

items: Each step is **one short clock cycle**
Different instructions use **different numbers** of cycles
The **same ALU and memory** are reused in different cycles

steps.why: Short cycles and reused hardware are the two gains.
steps.real: Many microcontrollers still work this way: the processor takes several clocks per instruction.

steps.title: Building the multi-cycle datapath

blocks.text: Compare it with the single-cycle datapath: there is **one memory** and **one ALU**. Intermediate registers separate the steps, and multiplexers choose what each shared unit sees in each cycle.

steps.why: One memory and one ALU save hardware; the intermediate registers make that sharing possible.

steps.title: Build it up

steps.text: **One memory** holds both instructions and data. The **PC** addresses it. What comes out is saved in an **instruction register (IR)** or a **memory data register (MDR)**.
The **register file** reads two registers into **A** and **B**. Intermediate registers hold values between cycles, because the next cycle reuses the same hardware.
**One ALU** does every calculation: PC + 4, the memory address, the arithmetic and the branch comparison. **ALUOut** holds its result. Multiplexers choose the inputs.
Extra paths: the PC can be loaded from the ALU or ALUOut; ALUOut can address memory; B supplies the data for a store.
The **control unit** is now a **finite-state machine**: its state tells the datapath what to do in the current cycle.

steps.why: Each click adds a group of components. Compare with the single-cycle datapath from Class 10.

steps.title: Follow lw and add

steps.text: The complete diagram. Pick a scenario and press Play or Step.
**Cycle 1, fetch**: IR = Mem[PC] and the ALU computes PC + 4, which is written back to the PC.
**Cycle 2, decode**: read $s1 into A and $t0 into B; sign-extend the offset. (The ALU can also precompute the branch target.)
**Cycle 3, address calculation**: the ALU adds A + 8 and keeps the result in ALUOut.
**Cycle 4, memory read**: ALUOut addresses the memory; the data is saved in MDR.
**Cycle 5, write back**: the MDR is written into $t0. The instruction took five cycles.
**Cycle 1, fetch**: read the instruction; PC = PC + 4.
**Cycle 2, decode**: read $s1 into A and $s2 into B.
**Cycle 3, execute**: the ALU adds A and B; ALUOut holds the sum.
**Cycle 4, write back**: ALUOut is written to $t0. Four cycles: the memory stage is skipped.

steps.why: Run the lw scenario: five cycles, and the ALU is used three times (PC + 4, the address calculation, and sometimes the branch target).

steps.title: What is a finite-state machine?

items: A set of **states**: one per step of an instruction
The machine is in **one state per clock cycle**
Each state sets the **control signals** for that cycle (outputs)
The **next state** depends on the current state and the opcode (input)

blocks.text: S0 and S1 are the same for every instruction. At S1 the opcode picks the path.

steps.why: The control unit becomes a small machine that steps through states instead of a single block of logic.
steps.real: Traffic lights and vending machines are also finite-state machines.

explainAgain.beginner: A board game: you are always on one square (state); the dice (opcode) decide which square is next.

steps.title: The states, built up

steps.text: Every instruction starts with **Fetch** and **Decode**: the same two states for all.
**lw and sw** share the address calculation. lw then reads memory and writes the register; sw writes memory.
**R-type** instructions execute in the ALU and write their result.
**beq** needs a single extra cycle to compare and update the PC. Every path ends back at Fetch.

steps.why: The branching happens at S1, once the opcode is known.

steps.title: Walk each instruction through

steps.text: The complete diagram. Pick a scenario and press Play or Step.
**S0**: fetch. Every instruction starts here.
**S1**: decode. The opcode decides the next state: lw goes to S2.
**S2**: compute the address A + offset.
**S3**: read memory into the MDR.
**S4**: write the MDR into the register, then return to S0. Total 5 cycles.
**S0**: fetch.
**S1**: decode.
**S2**: compute the address A + offset.
**S5**: write register B into memory, then return to S0. Total 4 cycles.
**S0**: fetch.
**S1**: decode.
**S6**: the ALU computes A op B.
**S7**: write ALUOut to rd and return. Total 4 cycles.
**S0**: fetch.
**S1**: decode (the branch target is already computed).
**S8**: compare A and B; if equal, PC = target. Total 3 cycles.

steps.why: Run all four scenarios and count the states each one visits: that is its cycle count.

steps.question: Which states does `sw` pass through?

reveal.text: Fetch (S0), decode (S1), address (S2), then memory write (S5): **4 cycles**.

steps.result: lw is S0, S1, S2, S3, S4; R-type is S0, S1, S6, S7; beq is S0, S1, S8.

steps.title: Single-cycle vs multi-cycle

head: Single-cycle
Multi-cycle
rows: An instruction can use multiple cycles

steps.why: The multi-cycle design trades more cycles per instruction for a shorter cycle and shared hardware.
steps.real: Choosing between the two is a classic architecture trade-off: neither is simply better.

steps.title: Which is faster? Calculate

blocks.title: Single-cycle vs multi-cycle (illustrative delays)
blocks.equation: Time per instruction = CPI × clock period

steps.why: The delays are illustrative. With the defaults the multi-cycle design needs 4.05 cycles × 200 ps = 810 ps per instruction, almost the same as the 800 ps single-cycle design. Change the delays and the mix: the winner depends on the balance of the steps and on the instruction mix.

steps.question: With these delays and the 25/10/45/20 mix, which design finishes an instruction faster on average?
options: About the same: 800 ps (single) vs 810 ps (multi)

reveal.text: Multi-cycle: CPI 4.05 × 200 ps = **810 ps**. Single-cycle: **800 ps**. The shorter clock is cancelled by the extra cycles.

steps.result: The multi-cycle benefit is mostly hardware reuse; the next class (pipelining) is what gets the clock and the CPI together.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: If multi-cycle is not faster here, why would a designer still choose it?
steps.answer: It saves hardware: one memory and one ALU instead of two memories and three adders. It also lets slow operations (multiply, divide, slow memory) take extra cycles without slowing every instruction, and it sets the stage for pipelining, which overlaps these cycles.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: What would you need to change so that multi-cycle clearly beats single-cycle?
ideas: More balanced step delays, so the clock period gets close to one fifth of the total.
An instruction mix with more short instructions (beq, jumps).
Slow, rare instructions (multiply) that single-cycle would have to fit in every cycle.
Overlapping the steps of different instructions: pipelining.

steps.question: Name the five intermediate registers of the multi-cycle datapath.
steps.answer: IR, MDR, A, B and ALUOut.
steps.solution: They hold the instruction, memory data, the two operands and the ALU result between cycles.

steps.question: How many cycles do `add`, `lw`, `sw` and `beq` take?
steps.solution: add: fetch, decode, execute, write back. lw: plus memory read. sw: memory write, no write back. beq: fetch, decode, branch.
steps.hint: Which steps does each instruction skip?

steps.question: Give the path through the control FSM for an R-type instruction and the cycle count.
steps.solution: Fetch, decode, execute in the ALU, then write the result to rd.
steps.hint: Which states do R-type instructions skip?

steps.question: A program has 1,000 instructions with CPI 4.05 and the clock period is 200 ps. How long does it take?
Mix: 30% lw, 10% sw, 40% R-type, 20% beq (cycles 5, 4, 4, 3). Clock = 200 ps. What are the CPI and the time per instruction? Compare with a single-cycle design at 800 ps.
steps.answer: CPI 4.1; 820 ps per instruction; single-cycle (800 ps) is slightly faster.
steps.mistake: Averaging the cycle counts without weighting them by frequency.
steps.title: Exam practice: numerical

steps.question: Trace `beq $t0, $t1, L` (the registers are equal) through the FSM. Give each state and the action.
steps.answer: S0 fetch (IR = Mem[PC], PC = PC + 4); S1 decode (read A and B, compute the target into ALUOut); S8 (A = B, so PC = ALUOut). 3 cycles.
steps.solution: The target is computed in S1 so S8 only has to compare and update the PC.
steps.mistake: Taking 4 cycles by adding a write-back state.
steps.title: Exam practice: state tracing

steps.question: `lw $t0, 8($s1)` has $s1 = 0x1000 and Mem[0x1008] = 42. Give the values of ALUOut, MDR and $t0 after cycles 3, 4 and 5.
steps.answer: After cycle 3: ALUOut = 0x1008. After cycle 4: MDR = 42. After cycle 5: $t0 = 42.
steps.solution: Cycle 3 adds 0x1000 + 8 = 0x1008. Cycle 4 reads memory at that address into MDR. Cycle 5 writes MDR to $t0.
steps.mistake: Putting the memory data directly in ALUOut.
steps.title: Exam practice: datapath tracing

steps.question: Explain two advantages and one weakness of the multi-cycle processor compared with the single-cycle one.
steps.answer: Advantages: a shorter clock cycle, and shared hardware (one memory, one ALU) instead of duplicates; simple instructions also finish in fewer cycles. Weakness: every instruction needs several cycles (CPI above 1) and extra registers and control states, so the total time is not necessarily shorter.
steps.solution: A strong answer states the trade-off between cycle length and cycle count.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: Single-cycle: the clock is set by lw and hardware is duplicated.
Multi-cycle: one step per cycle, one memory and one ALU reused.
Intermediate registers: IR, MDR, A, B, ALUOut carry values between cycles.
The control unit is a finite-state machine: S0 fetch and S1 decode for all, then the opcode picks the path.
Time per instruction = CPI × clock period; multi-cycle is not automatically faster.

mistakes.wrong: Multi-cycle is just single-cycle with a slower clock.
mistakes.right: It is a redesigned datapath with shared units and intermediate registers.

mistakes.wrong: All instructions take the same number of cycles.
A shorter clock always means a faster processor.
mistakes.right: Time = CPI × clock; more cycles can cancel the shorter clock.

mistakes.wrong: The ALU result goes straight to memory.
mistakes.right: It is held in ALUOut first.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Multi-cycle processors split each instruction into short steps and reuse one memory and one ALU. Intermediate registers (IR, MDR, A, B, ALUOut) pass values between cycles and a finite-state machine supplies the control signals. R-type and sw take 4 cycles, lw 5 and beq 3. The shorter clock does not guarantee a faster processor, since time per instruction is CPI times the clock period.
